senses: In Ancient Greece, a raised platform within the agora, where goods were displayed for sale.
Japanese amberjack, Pacific yellowtail (Seriola quinqueradiata).
A box containing a source of light and a white, translucent cover, used to view photographic transparencies.
A box containing fluorescent tubes or LED technology, used to treat people with seasonal affective disorder (SAD) and circadian rhythm disorders.
A kind of pop-up that is overlaid across a web page while the rest of the content is dimmed.
A device used in phreaking that indicates when a telephone line is in use by means of a light.
ety: From light + box. In the Internet sense, originally the name of one specific technique.

senses: Overweight and fortunate with one's life.
ety: From fat (“overweight”) + happy (“fortunate”). First attested in 2002.

senses: Meat from a young goat; kid.
examples: Mutton rivaled beef in prominence until this century, and cabrito, or kid, remains a major food in Nuevo León.

Mr. Dean O. Smith, who is the game warden in the Dripping Springs area, barbecues the cabrito for us, and what a treat that is! Cabrito is a very young Spanish goat between one and a half and two years old.
Consuela and Sullivan had been cooking all night so there was plenty of beef and cabrito.

senses: Any cod, pollock, haddock, or other whitefish.
ety: One theory derives it from scrawed, past participle of Cornwall dialect scraw (“to split and dry fish”), but the further origin of this word seems not to have been traced. Another theory derives it from an obsolete Dutch term: either from schrood (“slice, shred”), from Middle Dutch schrode, schroode, referring to the splitting of the fish; or alternatively from the related schrot (“inferior product, cull”), the scrod being originally a cod too small for filleting. In both of these cases, the word is ultimately cognate to shred. Compare East Frisian schrod (“small or worthless thing; shred”), G

senses: The initial roll of the dice in craps.
Having the ability to germinate
ety: From germinate + -ive. From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”) + -ate, from germinātus (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of germinō (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”).

senses: Explanatory; serving to explain logically or in detail.
ety: From Latin explicātīvus, from explicō (“to unfold, open out”).
examples: The witness was explicative in telling the police what he saw.

examples: Few channelers call themselves mediums, however, in part because the term conjures up an image of gypsy crones hunched over crystal balls, and in part because spiritualism has a history of fraud.

senses: Capable of being distributed

A tortoiseshell cat.
A traditional blouse worn by women in Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, and Southern Thailand.

common wormwood, mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris).
ety: From Middle English moderwort; equivalent to mother + wort. Compare Chinese 益母草 (yìmǔcǎo)

senses: A Viking grave marker taking the form of a recumbent monument, generally with a curved (hogbacked) ridge and outwardly curved sides.
An informal beach party in which food, usually seafood, is cooked in a firepit dug in the sand, filled with hot coals.
An avenging spirit or deity, variously associated with the Erinyes, Nemesis, and more.
In more recent ages, a term of rebuke for a pestilent rascal.
Someone or something that spangles.
One given to drinking alcoholic beverages too freely; a tippler.
ety: From bib (“drink heartily”) + -er (agent noun suffix); see bib (“clothing to prevent spills from mouth”). Bib is from Middle English bibben. First attested in the 1530s.

senses: The medregal (Seriola fasciata), an edible fish of the southern United States and the West Indies.
The cobia or crab eater (Rachycentron canadum), an edible fish of warm waters globally.

The particular value-theory of a philosopher, school of thought, etc.

senses: To propose or put forward for discussion or consideration.
ety: From Latin prōpōnō (“place before; offer, propose”), via Scots [Term?].

senses: A promenade or drive located beside the seashore in Hong Kong.
ety: Borrowed from Portuguese praia (“beach”). Doublet of playa and plage.
examples: Elsewhere on the Island, facilities for the transport of goods were limited to landing piers and prayas for junks and lighters.

senses: The act of expunging.

senses: A metacentric chromosome.
One who gelds or castrates.
ety: From Middle English geldere, equivalent to geld + -er.

senses: One thousandth (10⁻³) of an ampere. Symbol: mA.
A specialized type of material ropeway that incorporates a mechanism to raise and lower loads vertically from the suspended ropeway.
ety: From French blondin. Named after the French tightrope walker and acrobat Charles Blondin (1824–1897).
examples: His Irish labourers were accommodated on the north bank of the bridge when blondins were used to carry men and materials across the river.

senses: Bonding or joining of overlapping materials.
ety: Circa 1525, borrowed from Middle Dutch splissen (Modern Dutch splitsen); akin to Middle Dutch splitten (“to split”), German spleißen (“to split, splice”), Spliss (“split ends, hair breakage”), French épisser (also from Dutch). The Dutch word originally referred only to the fraying of the ropes' ends but was then also used for the entire process of fraying and retying; hence the peculiar semantic development from “split” to “join”. The same development occurred in German.

senses: Someone who participates in bobsled.

A female demon which comes to men, especially monks, in their dreams to seduce them and have sexual intercourse, drawing energy from the men to sustain themselves, often until the point of exhaustion or death.
A strumpet, whore or prostitute.
ety: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from alteration of Late Latin succuba (“strumpet, especially a mythological fiend in female form who has intercourse with men in their sleep”) based on incubus in Middle English, from Latin succubo (“to lie under”), from sub- (“under”) + cubare (“to lie down”).

senses: Malleable or flowing like plasma.
Involving the transformation from one form to another; metamorphic.
ety: From Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “anything formed or molded”) (genitive πλάσματος (plásmatos)) + -ic.
examples: Among the extraordinary features of the process of plasmatic modification, those are especially worthy of note that pertain to homogeneous terms of affection from which powers are subtracted.
The first of these is plasmatic in an obvious way; it suggests a delight in the impossible power of an ocean wave becoming something else.

senses: An early electronic amplifying tube consisting of a partially evacuated glass tube with three electrodes, a heated filament, a grid, and a plate.
ety: Neologism based on Latin audio (“to hear”).
